notes.meaning: Exodus begins by linking straight back to the story of Genesis. Jacob and his sons had moved to Egypt to find relief from a terrible famine, and each son brought his family along. God was caring for this small household before growing them into a great nation.

The sons of Jacob are listed by their mothers, naming the sons of Leah and Rachel first and then the sons of the servant wives. Joseph is not named in this group because he had already been living in Egypt. Every branch of Jacob's family had an important place in God's growing people.

Jacob's direct family who first settled in Egypt totaled only seventy people, including Joseph who was already there. Scripture records this small number so readers can contrast it with the massive nation that later walked out of Egypt. God can take a tiny, humble group and accomplish great things through them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that different ancient writers had different ways of counting the family, with one group counting seventy people without Jacob and another group including him.

notes.meaning: As the years passed, Joseph, his brothers, and everyone from that original generation died. Even though those leaders passed away, God's plan did not end with them. Human rulers and heroes come and go, but the Lord remains faithful across every generation.

The descendants of Israel multiplied quickly and filled the fertile land of Goshen where they lived. Scripture uses several words for growth to show that God was fulfilling His ancient promise to multiply Abraham's family. Even in a foreign country, God's blessing gave His people great life and strength.

A new king came to the Egyptian throne who had no personal memory of Joseph and no respect for his past service. This ruler started a new policy that treated the Hebrews as dangerous outsiders rather than honored guests. Earthly rulers easily forget past kindness, but the Lord never forgets His people.

Pharaoh told his royal advisers that the Israelites had become too large and powerful for Egypt to handle. He exaggerated their strength to make his people afraid and to build support for harsh actions against them. Worldly leaders often feel threatened when God blesses His people.

The king urged his leaders to act craftily so the Israelites would stop growing. He feared that if war broke out, the Hebrews would join Egypt's enemies, defeat them, and escape the land, costing Egypt a valuable workforce. What worldly rulers call clever planning is often just sinful opposition to God.

The Egyptians put harsh slave masters over the Israelites to crush their spirits with forced labor. Under these cruel overseers, the Hebrews built the supply cities of Pithom and Rameses to store grain and weapons for Pharaoh. Egypt thought brutal work would wear Israel out, but God was still watching over them.

Pharaoh's cruel plan failed because the more the Egyptians oppressed the Hebrews, the more the Hebrews grew and spread out. Seeing this rapid growth filled the Egyptians with dread and loathing. Human cruelty cannot stop the blessing and protection of God.

Instead of turning from their cruelty, the Egyptians made the Israelites work even harder and treated them without mercy. They used fierce demands and harsh punishments to try to break the strength of the people. Hardened hearts often become even more stubborn when their plans do not work.

The Egyptians made daily life miserable for the Hebrews through painful labor in mud, sun-dried brick, and heavy farm work. The work was exhausting, hot, and demanded without any kindness or rest. Even in this bitter suffering, God was preparing His people to long for the land He had promised them.

When forced labor did not stop Israel's growth, the king turned to a secret plot of murder. He called in Shiphrah and Puah, who were likely the head leaders of the midwives who helped women give birth. Scripture honors these humble women by naming them, while the powerful king remains unnamed.

Pharaoh commanded the midwives to check the sex of each baby during delivery on the birthstool. If the child was a boy, they were ordered to kill him immediately, but they were to let the girls live. Pharaoh wanted to destroy future Hebrew soldiers while keeping the women as powerless servants.

The midwives refused to carry out Pharaoh's murderous order because they feared God, holding deep reverence for Him as the true Judge and Creator. They knew taking innocent life was evil and that God's authority is higher than any earthly king's command. When human laws command what God forbids, believers must obey God rather than men.

Pharaoh noticed that Hebrew baby boys were still living, so he summoned the midwives to demand an explanation. Standing before the angry king placed the lives of these women in extreme danger. Even in the face of royal threats, they remained loyal to God.

The midwives answered that Hebrew women were strong and gave birth quickly before a midwife could even arrive. God had indeed blessed these mothers with quick, healthy deliveries during their hard labor. The midwives gave this answer to protect the infants and avoid obeying the king's bloody decree.

differ.view: Many in this tradition teach that the midwives told an untrue excuse, meaning that while their refusal to murder was holy, their deception was sinful and forgiven only by God's grace.
Some evangelicals hold that the midwives spoke the literal truth without lying, because the laboring Hebrew mothers truly experienced unusually quick births under God's special blessing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic moral teachers explain that God rewarded the midwives for their mercy and fear of the Lord, but not for using deception, since lying is never considered morally good.

notes.meaning: God treated the midwives with kindness because they honored Him and protected innocent lives. Meanwhile, the Israelite people continued to multiply and grow very strong despite the king's plans. God faithfully cares for those who stand up for the weak.

Because the midwives feared God, He blessed them personally by giving them families of their own. Since they protected the households of Israel, the Lord built up their own households in return. God never overlooks acts of faith and courage done for His people.

Having failed in his secret plots, Pharaoh gave an open command to all Egyptian citizens to drown every newborn Hebrew boy in the Nile River. He allowed the baby girls to live so they could be absorbed into Egypt. This cruel order brought great suffering, but it set the stage for God to raise up a deliverer.
